Marginal versus average tax: see the income slices before applying a rate

Use 2026 Canadian federal brackets in four graphics that explain income slices, the rate on the next dollar and the effect of an illustrative deduction.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

The central idea

A bracket rate applies to an income slice. Compare the tax on an additional amount with the average across the full amount, and keep this limited calculation separate from total tax or take-home pay.

01

Start with a clearly limited tax calculation

The Canada Revenue Agency’s 2026 federal table applies 14% to the first CAD 58,523, then 20.5%, 26%, 29% and 33% to successive bands ending at CAD 117,045, CAD 181,440, CAD 258,482 and above. Each rate applies to its own portion of taxable income.

This tool calculates that federal bracket arithmetic before credits. It does not apply the basic personal amount, other federal credits, provincial or territorial tax, Quebec abatement, CPP or EI, income-tested benefits or alternative minimum tax. Its result is not a tax-return estimate or take-home pay.

The starting input is taxable income before the one illustrative deduction entered in the controls. It is not necessarily gross salary. The model does not decide how salary, dividends, capital gains or other receipts enter taxable income, nor whether a particular deduction is available to a person.

02

Follow the amount charged within each band

The first graphic calculates the income falling between each lower and upper threshold, multiplies that portion by its rate, and displays the resulting tax. Bands above the selected income have zero amounts. The total is the sum of the slice taxes.

The default CAD 80,000 starting amount less an illustrative CAD 5,000 deduction leaves CAD 75,000 for the comparison. The first CAD 58,523 produces CAD 8,193.22 of bracket tax, and the remaining CAD 16,477 produces CAD 3,377.79 when rounded for display. The total is approximately CAD 11,571.01 before credits.

Applying 20.5% to all CAD 75,000 would discard the lower rate on the first band. Moving into the second band changes the rate on that next portion; it does not replace the rate previously applied to every earlier dollar.

03

Compare the next-dollar rate with the average

The stepped curve shows the bracket rate applying to the next dollar of taxable income. The average curve divides the calculated bracket tax by taxable income. At the default CAD 75,000, those figures are 20.5% and about 15.43% respectively, before credits.

At zero taxable income, the average ratio has a zero denominator and is not defined. The calculator reports that explicitly, and the average curve begins at CAD 1. Because credits are excluded, the curve below the first threshold is not a representation of the effective tax actually paid by a low-income household.

The rates shown are also not a person’s combined effective marginal rate. Provincial taxes, credits and changes in benefits can alter the effect of additional income. Use these curves to understand the bracket mechanism, then use a complete, current calculation for the actual household question.

04

Read what changes when income rises

The stacked bars compare the selected amount with the amount after adding the extra taxable income. The same illustrative deduction applies in both cases. One component is bracket tax before credits; the other is taxable income less only that tax.

In the default case, adding CAD 10,000 keeps that additional amount within the 20.5% band. It adds CAD 2,050 of federal bracket tax and CAD 7,950 to the arithmetic remainder. The remainder omits the other taxes, deductions and benefit effects listed above, so it should not be labelled a paycheque.

The graph illustrates why a higher bracket rate does not automatically absorb all of a raise. It does not establish the after-tax value of a specific employment offer or the tax consequences of a transaction.

05

A deduction may span several bands

The matrix compares illustrative deductions at several taxable-income amounts. Each cell is the difference between bracket tax before and after the deduction. If the deduction crosses a threshold, its portions affect tax at different rates; multiplying the full deduction by one headline rate may then be inaccurate.

The selected input deduction is applied once and taxable income is floored at zero. The fixed grid supplies its own alternative income and deduction amounts. It does not determine deductibility, carryforward treatment, refunds or the effect of credits.

The rules in this article are fixed to 2026 and were reviewed on 25 October 2026. Recheck the applicable year and the full federal and provincial rules before using a tax assumption in a contribution, withdrawal or employment decision. A clear distinction between bracket arithmetic and a complete tax calculation keeps the planning comparison understandable.
